svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Cross-Cloud Interconnect differs from the two Interconnect options before it in Google Cloud; it is a product in which Google provisions a dedicated physical connection between the Google network and that of another cloud service provider, inverting the Dedicated Interconnect arrangement where you supply your own routing equipment in a colocation facility; the supported remote providers being Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Alibaba Cloud, which the documentation calls your remote cloud service provider; port sizes that are not uniform, with 10, 100 and 400 gigabits for AWS and OCI but only 10 and 100 for Azure and Alibaba, so the top speed of 400 is 40 times the 10 gigabit entry size; connections bought in pairs, with 99.9 percent needing a primary and a redundant connection in different edge availability domains of one metropolitan area and 99.99 percent needing either two pairs across two metros using two domains in each, or a single-region topology with both Cloud Routers in the same region on attachments in different domains; the definition of an edge availability domain as a zone within a metropolitan area where two domains are typically not down for maintenance at once; the comparison with the partner variant, where you own the connections outright and cannot share them whereas partner ports are owned by Google and the other provider and shared between customers, with granular speeds from 1 to 50 gigabits and no data transfer fee; and the support boundary, where Google supports the connection as far as the other provider's demarcation
svg.title: Cross-Cloud Interconnect: Google builds the link, and support stops at the other cloud's demarcation
svg.text: The one where Google lays the cable — the exact inverse of #87.
Dedicated made you bring routers to a colocation facility. Here Google provisions the link.
What you are actually buying
WHEN YOU BUY CROSS-CLOUD INTERCONNECT, GOOGLE PROVISIONS A DEDICATED PHYSICAL CONNECTION
between the Google network and that of another cloud service provider.
No colocation contract, no optics budget, no 10 km radius, no cross-connect to order.
Supported remote providers: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Alibaba Cloud.
Port sizes are NOT uniform across providers — check before you design
AWS and OCI: 10 Gbps, 100 Gbps, and 400 Gbps
Microsoft Azure, Alibaba: 10 Gbps, 100 Gbps
400 Gbps is 40x the 10-Gbps entry size — and it is unavailable on half the providers.
99.9% — production non-critical
• MINIMALLY TWO connections: one
primary, one redundant
• Each in a DIFFERENT edge availability
domain of a metropolitan area
• One metro is enough
Connections are bought in PAIRS.
99.99% — production critical
MULTI-REGION:
• TWO PAIRS of connections
• Each pair in a DIFFERENT metro
• Two edge domains WITHIN each metro
SINGLE-REGION also reaches 99.99%:
• Both Cloud Routers in the SAME region,
on attachments in different domains
The maintenance fact, finally stated as a definition
An edge availability domain is a ZONE WITHIN A METROPOLITAN AREA. Using several maximizes
availability because two domains in the same metro are typically not down for maintenance together.
CROSS-CLOUD INTERCONNECT
• Connections FULLY OWNED BY YOU and
cannot be shared across organizations
• Speeds: 10, 100, 400 Gbps
• Needs physical provisioning
• You pay for ports and attachments in
BOTH CLOUDS, plus data transfer out
• Support to the remote demarcation
PARTNER CROSS-CLOUD (OCI)
• Google Cloud and OCI own the ports;
connections shared by many customers
• No physical provisioning
• Partner attachments and virtual
circuits — NO DATA TRANSFER FEE
• Supported end to end, jointly
Two boundaries worth writing into the design document
SUPPORT: Google supports the connection all the way to the remote provider’s DEMARCATION —
and no further. #88’s SLA boundary, restated as a support boundary.
MTU: jumbo frames are configurable with any provider, but the remote cloud’s limits MAY NOT
MATCH Google’s. Read their documentation, not this one, for the far end.
FEASIBILITY FIRST: connections are supported only in certain locations. Check before designing anything.
